title: Roman love - Works in Progress Magazine
gist: Drawing on Kyle Harper's From Shame to Sin, the piece argues Roman sexual 'tolerance' was a status privilege of free men over slaves, women and the penetrated (codified in the Lex Scantinia), while Christianity, despite deep hostility to desire, invented exclusive mutual fidelity and extended moral concern to the rightless, e.g. the 428 law against coerced prostitution. It asks whether the fidelity norm will survive Christianity's decline in Europe.

insights.claim: The popular narrative that classical Antiquity had a tolerant, affirmative sexual culture crushed by repressive Christianity is, per Kyle Harper's From Shame to Sin, not entirely wrong but so incomplete as to be fundamentally misleading.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Popular historical narratives used to frame cultural change can be badly incomplete; check the selective structure behind 'permissiveness'.

insights.claim: Free Roman men were permitted sex with male and female slaves and prostitutes, including children, and male extramarital sex was considered acceptable in principle, with no norm of male fidelity.

insights.so_what: Roman 'permissiveness' was a privilege of status, not a general liberty.

insights.claim: Although only a small minority of Romans owned slaves, widespread prostitution of slaves made coerced sex ubiquitous, and the price of sex in the Roman Empire was about that of a loaf of bread.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Illustrates how a small owner class can shape mass-market norms via commodified coerced labor.

insights.claim: Roman permissiveness was highly selective: women had to be virgins at marriage and faithful afterward, lesbianism was treated with contempt, and many women in Greek-speaking provinces appear to have worn face veils in public.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Liberal-seeming societies can hold sharply asymmetric norms by gender.
insights.quote: Roman permissiveness was highly selective, however.

insights.claim: The Lex Scantinia likely punished both men who penetrated a free Roman man or boy and men who consented to being penetrated, meaning supposed Roman tolerance of homosexuality was strictly a licence for free men to penetrate unfree ones, whose status approximated 'breathing furniture'.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Norms that look like tolerance were in fact status-hierarchy enforcement.

insights.claim: Early Christians combined the Jewish prohibition of extramarital sex (which allowed polygamy) with Roman monogamy (which allowed male infidelity) to invent the ideal that each man should be faithful to one woman, just as each woman to one man.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: A major durable social institution emerged from the recombination of two pre-existing norm systems.
insights.quote: One result was the invention of male fidelity.
insights.locator: Christianity overthrew nearly all these norms.

insights.claim: It is not clear that the ideal of exclusive mutual fidelity was ever invented independently in any other major civilization, though it later spread to many non-Christian cultures.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Norms taken as universal may be historically contingent exports of one tradition.
insights.quote: it is not clear that the ideal of exclusive mutual fidelity has ever been invented independently in any other major civilizations

insights.claim: Whether the norm of exclusive mutual fidelity will survive Christianity's decline among European peoples is an open question the author poses.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Secularization may erode institutions (marriage norms, family structure) that were built on religious foundations, with demographic and social knock-on effects.
insights.quote: Perhaps we shall live to know if its hold over the European peoples survives Christianity’s decline.
insights.locator: Christianity overthrew nearly all these norms.

insights.claim: John Chrysostom explicitly redefined adultery to include a married man's affair with a prostitute or slave girl, and Pelagius stated that laws were made by men and disposed against women, showing early Christians knew they were radical.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Moral innovations often are self-consciously framed against prevailing elite norms.

insights.claim: Although Christianity grounds moral status in relationship to God rather than social position, most early Christians accepted slavery unquestioningly; Gregory of Nyssa was the great exception and the first recorded abolitionist in history.

insights.claim: In 428 the Christianized Imperial government forbade pimps, fathers and slave-owners from selling women for involuntary sex, punishing offenders with the public mines, and also offered free women forced into prostitution by poverty recourse to bishops, judges or municipal defensors.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: An early example of state regulation shifting from status-based to consent-based harm.

insights.claim: Christian sexual restrictiveness was motivated not only by negativity about desire but also by extension of moral concern to the rightless people of the classical world, though haphazardly and with predatory practice often continuing under a veneer of Christianization.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Restrictive norms can carry embedded protective functions that are lost when the norms are discarded.

insights.claim: Living for almost seventeen centuries under the 'Christian illusion' surely changed European peoples, the author argues, invoking Orwell's line that a mask can alter the expression of a face.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: Long-lived ideals shape behavior even when imperfectly practiced; their removal may have under-appreciated effects.

insights.claim: Early Christian writers were relentlessly negative about sexual desire, viewing it at best as a morally neutral animal appetite and more commonly as intrinsically sinful, ranking virginity above marriage; the idea of desire as ennobling emerged only in the Middle Ages.
insights.speaker: WorksInProgMag
insights.so_what: On this dimension the popular 'austere fanatics' image of early Christians is accurate.
